solution:
Sodium amalgam.

An alloy in which one of the metals is mercury is called an amalgam: "When one of the metals in an alloy is mercury the alloy is called amalgam. For example, sodium amalgam, zinc amalgam, etc."

Bauxite, whose formula is \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot n\text{H}_2\text{O}\).

The chapter states that "Aluminium is extracted from its ore bauxite \(\text{(Al}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot n\text{H}_2\text{O)}\)" and that bauxite is the main ore of aluminium, containing 30% to 70% \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\).

Aluminium oxide, \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\) (alumina) - an amphoteric oxide.

An amphoteric oxide reacts with both an acid and a base to give a salt and water. The chapter names alumina as amphoteric while describing Bayer's process: "Aluminium oxide being amphoteric in nature, it reacts with the aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide to form water soluble sodium aluminate."

[Note: the chapter prints only the base side of this behaviour, the reaction of alumina with sodium hydroxide. It does not print the corresponding reaction with an acid. Zinc oxide is also amphoteric, but the chapter never describes it as such, so alumina is the oxide this chapter supports as the answer.]

Ball mill.

The chapter refers to it twice: the powdered ore fed to the Wilfley table is "obtained from lumps of the ore using ball mill", and in Bayer's process "the ore is first ground in a ball mill".

Graphite.

Nonmetals are generally bad conductors, but the chapter records this exception: "Graphite, an allotrope of carbon, is an exception, as it is a good conductor of electricity."

Aqua regia.

The chapter defines it as "a highly corrosive and fuming liquid. It is one of the few reagents which can dissolve the noble metals like gold and platinum", freshly prepared by mixing concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the ratio 3:1.

| Substance | Property |
|---|---|
| a. Potassium bromide | 2. Soluble in water |
| b. Gold | 4. High ductility |
| c. Sulphur | 1. Combustible |
| d. Neon | 3. No chemical reaction |

Reasons, from the chapter:

- **Potassium bromide** is an ionic compound, and "Ionic compounds are water soluble", because water molecules orient around the ions set free by dissociation.
- **Gold** is a metal, and metals "have the properties namely, ductility and malleability".
- **Sulphur** is a nonmetal that burns in oxygen: \(\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{SO}_2\) (an acidic oxide), so it is combustible.
- **Neon** is a noble gas, and "Noble gases (like helium, neon, argon) do not take part in the chemical reactions" because their outermost shell is complete.

| Group A (ore) | Group B (metal) |
|---|---|
| a. Bauxite | ii. Aluminium |
| b. Cassiterite | iii. Tin |
| c. Cinnabar | i. Mercury |

Each pairing is stated in the chapter: "Bauxite is the main ore of aluminium"; "cassiterite is a tin ore. It contains mainly the nonmagnetic ingredient stannic oxide \(\text{(SnO}_2)\) and the magnetic ingredient ferrous tungstate \(\text{(FeWO}_4)\)"; and the chapter asks students to find out "how mercury is extracted from its ore cinnabar".

Metallurgy: "The science and technology regarding the extraction of metals from ores and their purification for the use is called metallurgy."

The chapter also describes the whole sequence that the word covers: the ore is mined, the gangue is separated from it (usually at the mine itself), the metal is then extracted in pure form, and the metal is finally purified by various methods. "This entire process is called metallurgy."

Ores: "The minerals from which the metal can be separated economically are called ores."

So every ore is a mineral, but only those minerals from which extraction is economically worthwhile are called ores. Ores also carry impurities such as soil, sand and rocky substances.

Minerals: "The compounds of metals that occur in nature along with the impurities are called minerals."

The chapter's context for this is that most metals are reactive and therefore do not occur free in nature, but are found combined as oxides, carbonates, sulphides and nitrates.

Gangue: the impurities present in an ore. "Ores contain many types of impurities such as soil, sand and rocky substances along with the metal compounds. These impurities are called gangue."

Removing the gangue is the first stage of metallurgy, called concentration of ores.

Copper vessels left in air for a long time acquire a greenish layer. The chapter identifies it: "Carbon dioxide in moist air reacts with the surface of copper vessel. Copper loses its luster due to formation of greenish layer of copper carbonate \(\text{(CuCO}_3)\) on its surface. This is called patination of copper."

Copper carbonate is a basic salt, so it is dissolved away by an acid. Lemon juice and tamarind are acidic, and on rubbing them over the vessel they react with the copper carbonate layer and remove it, so the vessel regains its lustre.

[Note: the chapter names the greenish layer as copper carbonate, but it does not itself state that lemon and tamarind are acidic or name the acids they contain. That step is carried over from the earlier work on acids.]

An ionic compound is built from cations and anions held together by the electrostatic force of attraction between opposite charges, and "The electrostatic attraction in the neighbouring ions with opposite charges is very strong."

To melt the compound this attraction has to be overcome, and the chapter states the consequence directly: "The intermolecular force of attraction is high in ionic compounds and, large energy is required to overcome it. Therefore, the melting and boiling points of ionic compounds are high."

The chapter's own table bears this out, giving melting points such as \(801\) for \(\text{NaCl}\) and \(2852\) for \(\text{MgO}\) in degrees Celsius, against \(0\) for water.

Sodium is one of the most reactive metals. It stands near the top of the reactivity series, and it "combines with oxygen in the air even at room temperature and forms sodium oxide":

\(4\text{Na}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{Na}_2\text{O}(s)\)

The chapter then gives the reason for the storage: "On exposure to air sodium readily catches fire. Therefore, to prevent accident in the laboratory or elsewhere it is kept in kerosene."

Sodium also "reacts rapidly and vigorously with water and liberates hydrogen gas", so kerosene serves to keep the metal away from both the oxygen and the moisture of the air. Kerosene does not react with sodium, so the metal can be stored under it safely.

The froth floatation method separates a sulphide ore from its gangue using two opposite properties: "the particles of the metal sulphides, due to their hydrophobic property, get wetted mainly with oil, while due to the hydrophilic property the gangue particles get wetted with water."

Pine oil is added for two reasons that the chapter gives. First, it is the oil that preferentially wets the sulphide particles, so that they can be lifted away from the gangue. Second, it is what makes the foam: "Certain vegetable oil such as pine oil, eucalyptus oil is added in the water for the formation of froth."

Pressurised air is blown through the water and the mixture is agitated, so a foam of oil, water and air bubbles forms and rises to the surface, carrying the sulphide ore particles with it, while the water-wetted gangue settles down.

In the electrolytic reduction of alumina the anodes are a set of graphite (carbon) rods dipped in the molten electrolyte, and oxygen is set free at the anode:

\(2\text{O}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4e^-\) (Oxidation)

That oxygen then attacks the anode itself. The chapter states the consequence: "The liberated oxygen reacts with the anodes to form carbon dioxide gas. The anodes have to be changed from time to time as they get oxidised during the electrolysis of alumina."

So the carbon of the anode is steadily burnt away as carbon dioxide, the anodes are gradually consumed, and they must be replaced from time to time.

A copper coin dipped in silver nitrate solution acquires a glitter because copper displaces silver from the solution and the displaced silver is deposited as a shining layer on the coin.

The chapter's rule for this is: "If a metal A displaces another metal B from the solution of its salt then it means that the metal A is more reactive than the metal B." In the reactivity series (fig 8.5) copper stands above silver, so copper is the more reactive of the two and displaces silver from silver nitrate solution.

\(\text{Cu}(s) + 2\text{AgNO}_3(aq) \rightarrow \text{Cu(NO}_3)_2(aq) + 2\text{Ag}(s)\)

The silver set free settles on the coin and gives it the glitter, and the solution slowly turns blue because copper nitrate is formed in it.

[Note: the chapter does not print this particular equation. It prints and illustrates the same kind of displacement for iron in copper sulphate solution, where a copper coating forms on the iron nail.]

Metal A has the electronic configuration 2,8,1, so it has 11 electrons and is **sodium (Na)**. Metal B has 2,8,2, so it has 12 electrons and is **magnesium (Mg)**.

**Metal A, sodium, is the more reactive.** Sodium has a single electron in its outermost shell and loses it very readily to attain the configuration of the nearest noble gas, whereas magnesium has to lose two. This is why the reactivity series of the chapter (fig 8.5) places sodium above magnesium.

Reactions with dilute hydrochloric acid, in which both metals give the chloride salt and liberate hydrogen gas:

\(2\text{Na}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

\(\text{Mg}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

[Note: the magnesium equation is printed in the chapter. The sodium equation is not - the chapter gives sodium's reaction with water rather than with acid - so it is written here on the same pattern as the other metal-acid reactions the chapter does print.]

**Magnetic separation method** (chapter fig 8.10).

The diagram shows an electromagnetic machine: a conveyor belt running around two rollers, one nonmagnetic and one magnetic (electromagnetic), with a hopper feeding powdered ore onto the belt at the nonmagnetic roller and two collector vessels standing below the magnetic roller.

Labels to be shown on the diagram: **Powdered ore**, **Nonmagnetic roller**, **Magnetic roller**, **Conveyor belt**, **Nonmagnetic ingredient**, **Magnetic ingredient**, **Collectors**.

How it works, from the chapter: the belt is nonmagnetic and is made of leather or brass. "The particles of the nonmagnetic part in the ore are not attracted towards the magnetic roller. Therefore, they are carried further along the belt and fall in the collector vessel" placed away from the magnetic roller, while "the particles of the magnetic ingredients of the ore stick to the magnetic roller and therefore fall in the collector vessel near the magnetic roller."

[Note: the answer to this question is the drawing itself. The description above lists the parts and labels exactly as the chapter's figure prints them, so that the diagram can be reproduced.]

**Froth floatation method** (chapter fig 8.11).

The diagram shows a large floatation tank containing water mixed with pine oil, an agitator rotating about a vertical axis in the centre, and a pipe supplying pressurised air at the bottom. A layer of froth carrying the ore floats at the top and is drawn off, while the gangue settles at the bottom.

Labels to be shown on the diagram: **Water and Pine oil**, **Air supply**, **Agitator**, **Bubbles**, **Froth**, **Concentrated sulphide ore**, **Gangue**.

How it works, from the chapter: finely ground ore is put into the tank; a vegetable oil such as pine oil is added for the formation of froth; pressurised air is blown through the water and the agitator stirs it, so "a foam is formed from oil, water and air bubbles together". The foam rises and floats, and "Particles of certain sulphide ore float with the foam on water as they preferentially get wetted by the oil", while the gangue, wetted by water, sinks. The chapter gives zinc blend \(\text{(ZnS)}\) and copper pyrite \(\text{(CuFeS}_2)\) as ores concentrated this way.

[Note: the answer to this question is the drawing itself. The description above lists the parts and labels exactly as the chapter's figure prints them, so that the diagram can be reproduced.]

**Electrolytic reduction of alumina** (chapter fig 8.12).

The diagram shows a steel tank lined on the inside with graphite, holding the molten electrolyte, with a set of graphite rods dipped into it from above and connected to the positive terminal of the cell. The graphite lining is connected to the negative terminal. Molten aluminium collects as a layer at the bottom of the tank and runs out through an outlet.

Labels to be shown on the diagram: **Steel tank**, **Cathode (Graphite lining)**, **Anode (Graphite)**, **Mixture of alumina, cryolite and fluorspar**, **Molten aluminium**, **Outlet for molten aluminium**, and the positive and negative terminals of the cell.

How it works, from the chapter: alumina melts above \(2000\) degrees Celsius, so cryolite \(\text{(Na}_3\text{AlF}_6)\) and fluorspar \(\text{(CaF}_2)\) are added "to lower its melting point up to \(1000\)" degrees Celsius. On passing current, "Aluminium is deposited on the cathode ... Molten aluminium being heavier than the electrolyte, is collected at the bottom of the tank", and oxygen is liberated at the anode.

[Note: the answer to this question is the drawing itself. The description above lists the parts and labels exactly as the chapter's figure prints them, so that the diagram can be reproduced.]

**Hydraulic separation method** (chapter fig 8.9).

The diagram shows a tapering vessel, like the one used in a grinding mill, opening into a tank that tapers on its lower side. Powdered ore is fed in at the top, water is forced in as a jet from the lower side, the gangue leaves through an outlet on the upper side, and the concentrated ore is collected at the bottom.

Labels to be shown on the diagram: **powdered ore**, **ore suspension**, **gangue**, **water**, **concentrated ore**.

How it works, from the chapter: "Finely ground ore is released in the tank. A forceful jet of water is introduced in the tank from the lower side. Gangue particles are lighter and therefore they flow out along with the water jet from the outlet on the upper side of the tank and get collected separately. At the same time the heavy particles of the ore are collected at the bottom from the lower side of the tank." The chapter adds that the method "is based on the law of gravitation, wherein particles of the same size are separated by their weight with the help of water."

[Note: the answer to this question is the drawing itself. The description above lists the parts and labels exactly as the chapter's figure prints them, so that the diagram can be reproduced.]

Aluminium exposed to air is oxidised, and a thin layer of aluminium oxide forms on its surface:

\(4\text{Al}(s) + 3\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3(s)\)

The chapter records this among the effects of corrosion: "By oxidation of aluminium, a thin layer of aluminium oxide forms on it." Elsewhere it notes that this layer is useful, since it "obstructs the contact of the aluminium with oxygen and water. This prevents further oxidation", which is what the anodisation process deliberately thickens.

[Note: the chapter states that the oxide layer forms but does not print the balanced equation, which is written here.]

Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate solution:

\(\text{Fe}(s) + \text{CuSO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\)

This is the chapter's own activity: an iron nail is dipped in copper sulphate solution and a copper coating forms on it. The chapter concludes from it that "iron has displaced copper from copper sulphate. It means that metallic iron is more reactive than metallic copper." The blue colour of the copper sulphate solution fades as green ferrous sulphate is formed.

This is the thermit reaction. Aluminium, being the more reactive metal, reduces ferric oxide to iron:

\(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{Al} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe} + \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{heat}\)

The chapter prints this equation and notes that "The heat evolved in the above reaction is so large that the metal is formed in the molten state", which is why the reaction is used for thermit welding of rails.

Alumina is melted, with cryolite and fluorspar added to lower the melting point, and the melt is electrolysed. The electrode reactions the chapter prints are:

Anode reaction: \(2\text{O}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4e^-\) (Oxidation)

Cathode reaction: \(\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{Al}(l)\) (Reduction)

Aluminium is deposited at the cathode, which is the graphite lining of the tank, and oxygen is liberated at the graphite anodes. Taken together the two electrode reactions give the overall change:

\(2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow 4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2\)

[Note: the chapter prints the two electrode reactions. The overall equation is obtained by combining them and is not itself printed.]

Zinc oxide is a basic oxide, so it neutralises the acid to give the salt zinc chloride and water:

\(\text{ZnO}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{ZnCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

Note that no hydrogen is set free here. This is what distinguishes an oxide from the metal: the chapter prints the reaction of zinc **metal** with dilute hydrochloric acid, in which hydrogen gas is liberated, whereas the reaction of the **oxide** with the acid gives only salt and water.

[Note: the chapter does not print this equation. It prints the reaction of zinc metal with dilute hydrochloric acid, and it obtains zinc oxide separately, by the roasting and calcination of zinc ores. The equation above is written from the general behaviour of a metal oxide with an acid.]

During the extraction of aluminium the ore used is bauxite, \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot n\text{H}_2\text{O}\), the main ore of aluminium.

The useful ingredient in it is alumina, aluminium oxide \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\). The chapter states that "Bauxite contains 30% to 70% of \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\) and remaining part is gangue."

The gangue is the impurity that has to be removed. The chapter describes it as being "made up of sand, silica, iron oxide etc.", and names the impurities specifically as silica \(\text{(SiO}_2)\), ferric oxide \(\text{(Fe}_2\text{O}_3)\) and titanium oxide \(\text{(TiO}_2)\).

Aluminium is a reactive metal and so does not occur free in nature; it is the third most abundant element in the earth's crust, after oxygen and silicon.

During the extraction of aluminium the bauxite ore is concentrated by leaching, which is the first step of the extraction.

The chapter defines the method: "In this method the ore is soaked in a certain solution for a long time. The ore dissolves in that solution due to a specific chemical reaction. The gangue, however, does not react and therefore does not dissolve in that solution. So it can be separated."

Applied to bauxite, "bauxite is soaked in aqueous \(\text{NaOH}\) or aqueous \(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\) which dissolves the main ingredient alumina in it." The alumina passes into solution as water-soluble sodium aluminate while the gangue does not, so the two are separated by filtration. Leaching with sodium hydroxide is Bayer's method and leaching with sodium carbonate is Hall's method; in both, the concentrated alumina is finally obtained by calcination.

The chapter notes that leaching is the first step in the extraction of aluminium, gold and silver from their ores.

During the extraction of aluminium, Hall's process converts bauxite into pure alumina as follows.

The ore is powdered and then leached by heating with aqueous sodium carbonate in a digester, which forms water-soluble sodium aluminate:

\(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(s) + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{NaAlO}_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

The insoluble impurities are then filtered out. The filtrate is warmed and neutralised by passing carbon dioxide gas through it, which precipitates aluminium hydroxide:

\(2\text{NaAlO}_2(aq) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\)

The precipitate of \(\text{Al(OH)}_3\) is filtered, washed, dried and then calcined by heating at \(1000\) degrees Celsius to obtain alumina:

\(2\text{Al(OH)}_3 \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

All three equations are printed in the chapter. The last step, calcination, is common to both Hall's and Bayer's processes.

During the extraction of aluminium, heating the ore with concentrated caustic soda is Bayer's process, the other method of concentrating bauxite.

The ore is first ground in a ball mill. It is then leached by heating with a concentrated solution of caustic soda, \(\text{NaOH}\), at \(140\) to \(150\) degrees Celsius under high pressure for 2 to 8 hours in a digester. Alumina is amphoteric, so it reacts with the sodium hydroxide solution to form water-soluble sodium aluminate:

\(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(s) + 2\text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{NaAlO}_2(aq) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

The iron oxide in the gangue does not dissolve in aqueous sodium hydroxide and is separated by filtration. Silica, however, does dissolve, forming water-soluble sodium silicate.

The aqueous sodium aluminate is then diluted with water and cooled to \(50\) degrees Celsius, which precipitates aluminium hydroxide:

\(\text{NaAlO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{NaOH} + \text{Al(OH)}_3\)

Finally the precipitate is filtered, washed, dried and calcined at \(1000\) degrees Celsius to give alumina:

\(2\text{Al(OH)}_3 \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

[Textbook note: the chapter is internally inconsistent about where two of these metals belong. Fig 8.5 bands magnesium together with aluminium, zinc, iron, tin and lead in the "react with acids" group, while the prose on printed p102 lists "sodium, calcium and magnesium" among the reactive metals that are obtained by electrolysis of their molten chloride salts. Copper is contradicted outright: printed p104 states that "The metals in the middle of the reactivity series such as iron, zinc, lead, copper are moderately reactive", yet printed p105 treats copper's extraction under the heading "c. Extraction of less reactive metals", saying that the metals at the bottom of the series are less reactive and that copper is obtained from \(\text{Cu}_2\text{S}\) simply by heating in air. The grouping below follows the chapter's own extraction-route classification, which is the criterion by which its "Extraction of metals" section is organised.]

**Reactive metals: Na, Li, Ca, Mg**

These stand at the top of the reactivity series. They are so reactive that they cannot be obtained by reduction with carbon, and "Their extraction has to be done by electrolytic reduction. For example, the metals sodium, calcium and magnesium are obtained by electrolysis of their molten chloride salts." Sodium and potassium react even with cold water, and sodium combines with the oxygen of the air at room temperature.

**Moderately reactive metals: Zn, Fe**

These lie in the middle of the series. The chapter says "The metals in the middle of the reactivity series such as iron, zinc, lead, copper are moderately reactive. Usually they occur in the form of their sulphide salts or carbonate." Their ores are first converted to the oxide by roasting or calcination and the oxide is then reduced, usually with carbon.

**Less reactive metals: Cu**

Copper lies low in the series, below iron and zinc. The chapter places its extraction with the less reactive metals: copper is now found mainly as \(\text{Cu}_2\text{S}\), and "Copper is obtained from \(\text{Cu}_2\text{S}\) ore just by heating in air", with no separate reducing agent needed.
